title: The magnets of the Large Hadron Collider are colder than outer space

cover.alt: Blue cylindrical dipole magnets of the Large Hadron Collider lined up along the curved tunnel at CERN.

body: The LHC steers protons around a 26.7 km ring with about 10,000 superconducting magnets, which only work when their coils are cold enough to lose all electrical resistance. Some 96 tonnes of superfluid helium chill them to **1.9 K, about −271 °C**. Empty space is warmer: the cosmic microwave background that fills the universe sits at about 2.7 K. Inside those magnets, protons circle at 0.999999990 of the speed of light, lapping the ring 11,245 times a second.

slides.label: the magnets’ operating temperature, about −271 °C
slides.text: Colder than the 2.7 K afterglow of the Big Bang that fills the gaps between the galaxies.

slides.heading: How cold is cold?
slides.note: The cosmic microwave background is at 2.725 K; the magnets run at 1.9 K

slides.question: How many laps of the 27 km ring does a proton complete every second?
slides.explanation: 11,245 laps a second: at 0.999999990 of the speed of light, the protons are only about 3.1 m/s slower than light itself.

slides.question: Why must the LHC’s magnet coils be kept so cold?
options: To keep the beam pipe empty
slides.explanation: Below their critical temperature the coils lose all electrical resistance, so huge currents flow without heating and the magnets can bend protons moving at nearly the speed of light.
